segments.title: History as institutional memory for officers
segments.summary: Why historical study belongs in military and naval education when short modern courses and limited recent experience cannot preserve every operational lesson.
segments.body: History supplies institutional memory that a short officer course cannot carry by itself. Modern courses grew from the shortened programmes introduced during the Second World War, leaving curriculum debates framed as a choice between one subject and another. One proposed alternative is to add four or eight weeks so that officers can learn more without dropping existing material. Recent amphibious experience presents a related problem: postwar operations have mostly involved raids by small forces and precision strikes. That experience suits another raid, but it offers little preparation for a major assault or intervention. The Falklands War was larger than most recent operations, yet smaller than major Second World War amphibious operations. Historians preserve the larger cases that officers may need when no service can afford a permanent staff with current experience of operations on that scale.

evidence.note: The lecture connects shortened officer courses, postwar raiding experience, amphibious warfare, and institutional memory.

segments.title: Staff rides turn historical cases into amphibious planning questions
segments.summary: How staff rides complement books by turning historical cases into practical questions about beach capacity, assembly space, logistics, and the size of a force that can move inland.
segments.body: Books carry historical lessons to officers who learn readily by reading. Officers who learn by doing need another method: the staff ride. Historians, veterans where available, and knowledgeable serving officers take trainees across the ground and reconstruct the choices involved. For an amphibious landing, that means asking whether a beach is wide enough, whether enough routes lead inland, and whether the ground behind it can hold the logistics for the operation. A beach may accept one brigade at a time and still become a serious bottleneck when a larger force must land. A division-sized assault might fit where a major force would not. Modern exercises often land a company to simulate a brigade because conducting the full operation costs too much. Staff rides give officers historical cases at scales that current training budgets cannot reproduce.

evidence.note: The lecture contrasts reading with learning by doing, defines staff rides, and applies them to landing space, logistics, bottlenecks, the Falklands, and large-scale amphibious operations.
